title: Promises versus C# Task and ValueTask
hook: Promise and Task share the await mental model — start work, pause, resume when done. The scheduler underneath differs: JS Promise continuations are microtasks on one thread; C# Task continuations run on thread-pool threads and may hop threads unless SynchronizationContext marshals back.

blocks.text: A JavaScript **Promise** is a thenable object: pending, fulfilled, or rejected. A C# **Task** represents an async operation: running, ran to completion, faulted, or canceled. **await** in both languages pauses the current function until the operation completes. **Promise.all** maps to **Task.WhenAll** for concurrent waits. **AbortController** with **AbortSignal** is the practical JS analog of **CancellationToken** — cooperative, not preemptive. C# adds **ValueTask** for sync-complete hot paths; JavaScript always allocates a Promise from async functions.

entries.plainDefinition: Built-in async result object with microtask-scheduled continuations.
.NET reference type for async work with thread-pool continuations.
Struct that avoids Task allocation when result is already available — no JS equivalent.
Cooperative cancellation flag passed to fetch and other APIs.

blocks.text: Coming from C#, saying 'Task is just a Promise' misses the execution engine. A long CPU loop in a JS async function still blocks the single thread. In C#, other pool threads continue while one thread is busy — but blocking that thread with Task.Result still causes pool starvation in ASP.NET Core. JS has no ConfigureAwait — DOM access is safe on Promise continuations because they always run on the main thread. C# UI code needs SynchronizationContext or await without blocking.

blocks.title: Interview trap: async means parallel
blocks.body: await A then await B is sequential. Starting both then Promise.all / Task.WhenAll is concurrent wait — not parallel CPU unless you add Workers or Task.Run.

items.body: Both pause the function and resume on completion — different schedulers.

items.title: Combine independent work
items.body: JS: Promise.all([a, b]). C#: Task.WhenAll(a, b).

items.body: JS: controller.abort(). C#: cts.Cancel() on linked CancellationToken.

snippet.label: C# equivalent — Task.WhenAll
snippet.explanation: Lines 7–8: concurrent wait. Continuations may hop threads — unlike JS microtasks on one thread. Prefer await each result instead of .Result in production.

snippet.label: Cancellation — AbortController vs CancellationToken
snippet.explanation: Line 1–2: cooperative cancel after 30s — mirrors CancellationTokenSource.CancelAfter. Line 8: AbortError is expected cancel path, not a server 500.

snippet.label: Microtask ordering vs C# thread hop
snippet.explanation: JS Promise callbacks always same thread via microtasks. C# Task continuation Thread.CurrentThread.ManagedThreadId may differ after await.

blocks.title: Equating worker_threads with async/await
blocks.body: Worker threads are a separate JS thread — like Task.Run in C#. async/await alone does not parallelize CPU.

blocks.title: Using Task.Result after WhenAll in C# from JS mindset
blocks.body: In JS, awaiting resolved Promises is natural. In C#, .Result blocks and can deadlock UI — await each task instead.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: thread-affine resources matter. JS Promise continuation on main thread — safe for DOM. C# continuation on random pool thread — marshal to UI with SynchronizationContext. Under high I/O concurrency, C# scales across cores for independent continuations; JS serializes microtasks until Workers added. TypeScript Promise<T> is compile-time only — runtime is identical to JS.

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying Task is just a Promise without scheduler difference. Claiming C# await uses microtask queue. Equating worker_threads with async/await. Not knowing Promise.all and WhenAll overlap waits but do not parallelize CPU on one sequential chain.

interviewTakeaways: Promise and Task share programmer model — differ in scheduling: microtasks vs pool threads.
JS continuations stay on main thread — C# may hop unless context captured.
60s: Same await syntax, different engines. JS microtasks one thread. C# pool threads. WhenAll equals Promise.all. AbortSignal equals CancellationToken. ValueTask has no JS equivalent.
Follow-up: why can C# scale I/O concurrency differently than single-threaded Node for CPU-light workloads?
commonPitfalls: Weak: 'Task is just a Promise' — missing scheduler.
Weak: claiming C# await uses microtasks.
Strong: 'Same model, different scheduler. Microtasks vs pool. WhenAll equals Promise.all. Neither parallelizes CPU without Workers/Task.Run.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: TypeScript Promise<T> annotates JS Promise at compile time. Task<T> is a real CLR type with status and cancellation.
Promise.then and await continuations always microtasks on the JS thread — map against Task continuations on any pool thread.
